name: ss-geodata-mcp

tools.name: viewer_status
tools.description: Whether a viewer page is attached to this companion, which viewer build and data set it is, where it dialled from, and the last state event it pushed (settled, flight-ended, interrupted with its reason). Answers even with no page attached; call it first, and again whenever another tool reports "not-connected".

tools.name: viewer_capabilities
tools.description: The whole contract in one call, so nothing here has to be discovered by trying it: the argument-naming convention, the solar tokens a clock accepts, what the scene echo and the warnings channel carry, every refusal code and what to do about each, the session caps and what is used of them, and what building attribute coverage means. Needs no page for the conventions; with one attached it also reports the live caps and which layers this set publishes. Read this first in a fresh session rather than probing.

tools.name: viewer_state
tools.description: Camera, clock/season/sun, clouds, quality, layer toggles, which data sets exist, loading counters, film status ({playing, name, shot, t, total, owner, once} or null), the attribution strings to quote, the drawn lines with their settle state, the marks with hit/pending counts, and the registries. Read live.

tools.name: viewer_set_camera
tools.description: Places the CAMERA at lat/lon/alt. It does not aim at anything unless look_at is given — for "go to X" use viewer_go_to. A cut, not a flight: lat/lon WGS84 degrees, alt metres above the ellipsoid (120 m - 900 km), yaw compass degrees (0 north, 90 east), pitch degrees below the horizon (negative looks up, within +/-86); look_at {lat, lon, alt?} replaces yaw and pitch with the bearing and pitch to that point. The published set covers Japan only: lat 20-46, lon 122-154. Returns the camera the page settled on. Verify with viewer_screenshot.

pitch_deg.description: Degrees below the horizon, -86 to 86; negative looks up

alt.description: Metres above the ellipsoid; default the loaded ground there, else 0

look_at.description: A point to aim the camera at; overrides yaw and pitch

tools.name: viewer_fly_to
tools.description: Places the CAMERA at lat/lon/alt. It does not aim at anything unless look_at is given — for "go to X" use viewer_go_to. Flies there from the current camera over `fly_s`, splined; yaw_deg and pitch_deg omitted keep the current ones, look_at {lat, lon, alt?} replaces them with the bearing and pitch to that point. clock and season may each be a scalar or [from, to] scrubbed across the flight ("06:00" to "19:30" runs the day). Resolves when the flight ends; if it reports interrupted, the person took the camera — do not fly again without asking.

yaw_deg.description: Compass degrees; omitted keeps the current

pitch_deg.description: Degrees below the horizon, -86 to 86; omitted keeps the current

ease.description: One of linear | in | out | inout; default linear

clock.description: JST hours, "HH:MM", or a solar token (sunrise, golden_hour_pm, sunset-0:20 ...) resolved where this call is aimed; or [from, to] scrubbed across the flight

season.description: Day of year or "MM-DD"; or [from, to]

clouds.description: One of clear | scattered | fair | overcast

alt.description: Metres above the ellipsoid; default the loaded ground there, else 0

look_at.description: A point to aim the camera at; overrides yaw and pitch

caption.description: A caption shown during the flight and cleared after, at most 240 characters

tools.name: viewer_go_to
tools.description: Go to a place and LOOK AT it: flies to a viewpoint a little way off and aims the camera at the coordinates. Use this for "go to X", "show me X", "take me to X". viewer_fly_to is NOT this — it places the camera itself at the coordinates. The viewpoint stands distance_m (default 1500) from the place on bearing_deg (default: the side the camera is already on, so the flight approaches rather than swings round), looking down at pitch_deg (default 25). fly_s 0 cuts; the default 6 s flies. target_alt_m is the place's height; omitted, the loaded ground is used and the frame corrects itself once it loads. name instead of lat/lon goes to a BUILDING by its PLATEAU name (a station, a tower, a hall, a school: 東京スカイツリー, 神田駅, 区立常盤小学校): the name is looked up in the loaded cells and the set's national name index, an exact match is preferred among substring hits, and the camera aims 20 m above its roof. Coordinates are still the way for anything that is not a building (a summit, a bay, a district).

lat.description: The place, latitude 20-46 (with lon; or give name)

name.description: A building's name instead of lat/lon, 1-80 characters, matched case-insensitively as a substring; exact match preferred

distance_m.description: How far off the camera stands, 50-500000 m; default 1500

bearing_deg.description: Compass bearing from the place to where the camera stands; default the side the camera is on now

pitch_deg.description: Degrees the camera looks down, 0-86; default 25

fly_s.description: 0 = cut, else fly over 0.2-120 s; default 6

target_alt_m.description: The place's height, metres above the ellipsoid; default the loaded ground

clock.description: JST hours, "HH:MM", or a solar token resolved at this place; or [from, to] scrubbed across the flight

caption.description: A caption shown during the flight and cleared after, at most 240 characters

tools.name: viewer_frame
tools.description: viewer_go_to is this tool with defaults; use viewer_go_to for "go to X". Solves the camera from a SUBJECT you know the position of: the camera stands distance_m from the target along compass bearing_deg (bearing 0 = camera north of the target, looking south) and looks down at it at pitch_deg. fly_s 0 (default) cuts; otherwise it flies there from the current camera, with optional clock/season scrubs. target_alt_m is the subject's ellipsoidal height (a summit, a roof); when omitted the loaded ground under the target is used, and if none is loaded yet the frame is made at 0 m, the tiles are given a moment to arrive, and one corrective cut re-frames on the real ground. Returns the solved camera.

distance_m.description: Camera distance from the subject, 50-500000 m

bearing_deg.description: Compass bearing FROM the subject TO where the camera stands

pitch_deg.description: Degrees the camera looks down, 0-86; default 25

target_alt_m.description: Subject height, metres above the ellipsoid; default 0

clock.description: JST hours, "HH:MM", or a solar token resolved at this place; or [from, to] scrubbed across the flight

caption.description: A caption shown during the flight and cleared after, at most 240 characters

tools.name: viewer_orbit
tools.description: Flies an arc about a SUBJECT at constant radius, always looking at it: from start_bearing_deg (compass, where the camera begins relative to the subject) through sweep_deg (sign = direction, positive clockwise seen from above) over `fly_s`. approach_s > 0 first flies from the current camera to the arc's start. clock/season scrub across the arc. target_alt_m omitted = the loaded ground under the subject (with one corrective cut at the end if it only loaded during the orbit). Reports interrupted if the person took the camera; do not fly again without asking.

pitch_deg.description: Degrees the camera looks down, 0-86; default 25

start_bearing_deg.description: Compass bearing from the subject to the first camera; default 0

sweep_deg.description: Degrees of arc, -720 to 720, not 0; default 90

target_alt_m.description: Subject height, metres above the ellipsoid; default 0

ease.description: One of linear | in | out | inout

clock.description: JST hours, "HH:MM", or a solar token resolved at the subject; or [from, to] scrubbed across the arc

season.description: Scalar or [from, to] scrub across the arc

approach_s.description: Fly to the start of the arc first, over this many seconds; default 0

caption.description: A caption shown during the flight and cleared after, at most 240 characters

tools.name: viewer_nudge
tools.description: Relative camera moves — "a bit more to the left", "zoom in", "higher", "look down", "back up": yaw_deg turns the heading (positive = to the right), pitch_deg tips it (positive = look further down, negative = up), dolly multiplies the altitude (0.5 = twice as close, 2 = twice as far; 0.1-10), forward_m / right_m move along and across the current heading over the ground (negative = back / left), up_m changes the altitude in metres. Any combination, at least one; all deltas from the camera as it is now. Pauses a running reel like a move key. Returns the new camera; verify with viewer_screenshot.

yaw_deg.description: Turn the heading, degrees; positive = to the right (clockwise)

pitch_deg.description: Tip the view, degrees; positive = look further down

dolly.description: Altitude factor 0.1-10: below 1 closer, above 1 farther

forward_m.description: Move along the heading over the ground, metres; negative = back

right_m.description: Move across the heading, metres; negative = left

up_m.description: Change the altitude, metres; negative = down

tools.name: viewer_tour
tools.description: A narrated tour of several places as ONE reel: for each stop, a flight from the previous camera to a viewpoint that looks at the place (solved like viewer_go_to: distance_m default 1500, bearing_deg default the previous stop's, pitch_deg default 25), then a hold there of hold_s seconds carrying the caption. Per-stop clock/season are scrubbed across the flight from the previous stop's values. Returns at once with the plan; the reel then runs on the page. Use viewer_film action=wait to wait for it, or viewer_film stop to end it early. 1-24 stops.

bearing_deg.description: Where the camera stands, compass; default the previous stop's (first stop 180)

hold_s.description: Hold seconds, 0-120; default 4; 0 skips the hold

caption.description: Shown during the hold, at most 240 characters

clock.description: JST hours, "HH:MM" or a solar token at this stop; [from, to] scrubs across the flight in

season.description: Day of year, "MM-DD", or [from, to] at this stop

layers.description: Layer toggles applied as this stop begins, e.g. {"buildings": true, "nightlights": false}

theme.description: A viewer_theme_buildings argument object applied as this stop begins; null takes the tour's own theme off again

tools.name: viewer_play_shots
tools.description: Plays a playlist in the film schema: each entry is a shot object (keys, seconds, ease?, clock?, season?, clouds?) or the name of a scouted shot file such as "010-fuji-dawn" (see the ss-geodata://shots/ resources). Playlist-level clock, season and clouds apply to shots that set none. Returns at once with the film status; use viewer_film action=wait to wait for it.

shots.description: Shot objects and/or shot-file names, in order

clock.description: Playlist default clock, scalar or [from, to]

clouds.description: Playlist default clouds, one of clear | scattered | fair | overcast

tools.name: viewer_film
tools.description: Controls a playing reel: pause, resume, stop, next, prev, wait. wait blocks until the reel ends, is interrupted, or timeout_s (default 60, at most 600) passes, and reports which. The others return the film status.

action.description: One of pause | resume | stop | next | prev | wait

tools.name: viewer_render_film
tools.description: "Render a video / make an MP4 of this flight": writes the shot list (the same schema viewer_play_shots takes: shots of {name?, seconds, ease?, keys:[{lat, lon, alt, yaw?, pitch?, at?}], clock?, season?, clouds?, caption?}) into the shots directory and spawns the offline renderer (tools/film.js) DETACHED — this tool returns at once and the render runs for minutes to hours; viewer_film_jobs reports progress and runs the encode. The renderer opens its own Chrome against the serve, so a serve must be up (publish serve); no page connection is needed here. Frames land in film/frames/<name>/ and the MP4 in film/<name>.mp4. A killed or stalled render resumes by calling this tool again with the same name — frames already on disk are skipped. width sets the frame (height is 16:9); a 4K render (width 3840) is an overnight job — draft first at width 960, fps 10.

shots.description: Shot objects, in order (or give playlist)

playlist.description: A whole playlist {name?, shots:[...], clock?, season?, clouds?} instead of shots

name.description: The job's name, ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,60}$ — names the shot file, the frames directory and the MP4

width_px.description: Frame width in pixels, 320-3840; default 1920 (height is width*9/16)

encode.description: Encode the MP4 when viewer_film_jobs sees the render complete; default true

tools.name: viewer_film_jobs
tools.description: Progress of the offline renders viewer_render_film started (and any older ones on disk): frames done against the plan, whether the render still appears to be running (a frame written in the last two minutes), the log path, and the MP4 once it exists. When a job this session asked to encode is complete and has no MP4 yet, the encode is started here (detached, into the same log — if ffmpeg is missing, the log says so). Needs no page connection. name narrows to one job; a stalled job resumes via viewer_render_film with the same name.

name.description: One job by name; omitted, every job under film/frames

tools.name: viewer_caption
tools.description: A subtitle line over the viewer, at most 240 characters. seconds 0 (default) keeps it until cleared, otherwise it fades after that long (at most 3600). Empty text clears it.

text.description: The caption; empty clears. At most 240 characters

tools.name: viewer_add_markers
tools.description: Pins with labels at lat/lon: for summits, stations, anything that is not a building, and for naming what a mark points at. 1-64 per call, 80-character labels, color as #rrggbb or a CSS name. alt is metres ABOVE THE GROUND (default 0), resolved as the ground loads; ellipsoidal: true makes alt absolute instead. group names them for viewer_clear. Returns the ids added and the total placed.

alt.description: Metres above the ground (default 0), or above the ellipsoid when ellipsoidal is true

ellipsoidal.description: true: alt is absolute ellipsoidal metres; default false

tools.name: viewer_ground_height
tools.description: Heights of the loaded ground under up to 1024 points: h in ellipsoidal metres (like alt), sea in metres above sea level where the geoid is published, and finest when nothing better will come. null means the camera has not loaded that ground yet: fly there first (viewer_frame, viewer_fly_to) and ask again.

tools.name: viewer_preload
tools.description: Fetches the terrain under up to 256 places and waits for it, without moving the camera. Use it before framing, orbiting or measuring somewhere the camera has never been: a viewpoint solved over unloaded ground is framed at 0 m above the ellipsoid, which puts the camera inside any hill it was meant to look at. It fetches the coarsest published level — one tile per mesh, a real height, and the finer detail still arrives on its own once the camera is there. viewer_tour does this for its own stops, so a tour needs no warm-up call. Returns the heights, as viewer_ground_height does.

points.description: 1-256 places to fetch the ground under

timeout_s.description: Seconds to wait for the tiles, 1-60; default 15

tools.name: viewer_export_buildings
tools.description: Writes the buildings in a disc or a polygon to a GeoJSON file and returns the path and a summary — the matching set itself, not an aggregate of it, so it can go into a spreadsheet, a safety case or another tool. Takes the same selection as viewer_query_buildings (usage, height, ground, where). Each feature is a point at the centroid with the attributes as properties; footprints: true gives polygons instead, which is most of the bytes. Only loaded cells are exported — the summary says how many were not loaded, and flying closer or viewer_preload gets the rest. The file is written under exports/buildings; the text answer stays small on purpose, so read the file rather than asking for it back.

polygon.description: Instead of a disc: 3-256 points, a closed ring

min_height_m.description: Only buildings at least this tall, metres 0-2000

max_height_m.description: Only buildings at most this tall, metres 0-2000

min_ground_m.description: Only buildings whose ground is at least this far above sea level

max_ground_m.description: Only buildings whose ground is at most this far above sea level

footprints.description: Polygons instead of centroid points; default false

offset.description: Skip this many before the page; the answer says whether more remain

name.description: File name stem under exports/buildings; default from the place and the time

tools.name: viewer_coverage
tools.description: Which layers are published, which building attributes this set carries, and — with lat/lon — how many of the loaded buildings around that point actually have each one. Attribute coverage is a property of each city's PLATEAU delivery, not of the format: central Tokyo publishes no year and no structure where Sapporo publishes both, and absent is null, which no filter matches. Ask this BEFORE planning work that depends on an attribute — a pre-1981 seismic overlay needs year and structure, and finding out by theming a ward and seeing nothing colour in costs a flight. The set-level half needs no loaded tiles; the measured half counts what is loaded, so fly or viewer_preload there first for a true local answer.

lat.description: Where to measure coverage, latitude 20-46 (with lon); omitted gives the set-level answer only

radius_m.description: Disc to count over, 1-5000 m; default 1000

tools.name: viewer_pick
tools.description: The loaded ground under a point on the screen, as fractions of the frame (0-1; default the centre): lat/lon, h (ellipsoidal), sea, distance from the camera and the tile level — or the reason there is none. Also the nearest loaded footpath or steps within 30 m of the hit (N13 band 3; no names in the source). Buildings are not picked yet.

tools.name: viewer_identify
tools.description: "What is that building?" — the building under a screen point (x, y as fractions 0-1; default the centre of the frame), or the one at a coordinate (lat, lon: the footprint containing the point, else the nearest within radius_m, default 15, 1-200). Screen mode marches the pixel's ray down through the loaded LOD1 prisms, so a tower's roof pixel names the tower, not the ground behind it. Returns the name where PLATEAU gave one, usage decoded, height (structure height for a sliced tower), storeys, year, structure and fireproofing, hazard depths, ground above sea and the distance from the camera, plus the ground hit and any footpath there. Answers from loaded cells only: null with a reason means fly closer so the building cells load, then ask again.

x.description: Screen point, 0 = left edge, 1 = right; default 0.5. Not with lat/lon

y.description: Screen point, 0 = top edge, 1 = bottom; default 0.5

lat.description: A coordinate instead of a screen point, 20-46 (with lon)

radius_m.description: Coordinate mode: the nearest footprint within this many metres, 1-200; default 15

tools.name: viewer_describe
tools.description: "What am I looking at?" — one readable paragraph composed from the page: the camera (position, heading, pitch), the clock, date and sun, clouds, the layers on, any sea rise; the ground under the centre of the frame and the building there (as viewer_identify); the land cover within 500 m of that ground; the named buildings within radius_m (default 2000) of it, nearest first, up to 10; and the annotations on the page. Parts the page cannot answer (no ground loaded under the centre, no land-cover set, no names in this set) are said, not hidden. A compact numbers block follows the paragraph.

radius_m.description: How far around the centre ground to list named buildings, 1-5000 m; default 2000

tools.name: viewer_draw_line
tools.description: A line through 2-4096 lat/lon points, draped on the terrain: a route, a ridge, a border. color as #rrggbb or a CSS name, width_px 1-12 (default 4), style ghost | solid, group for viewer_clear. Returns the record with its 2D and 3D lengths, climb and descent, and how many of its samples have ground; where the camera has not been, the line lies on the ellipsoid until the tiles load.

tools.name: viewer_import_track
tools.description: Draws a GPS track from GPX XML you have fetched yourself. THE way to put a NAMED trail on the map (Trail 6, 稲荷山コース, a route out of a guidebook): the built-in N13 footpath layer has the geometry but no names, so it can only ever approximate a named route. Route-wiki sites such as Yamareco publish a GPX download per route — fetch one with your own web tools and pass the XML here. One line per <trkseg> (a segment break is a gap in the recording, so segments are never joined) and one per <rte>; <wpt> elements become markers in the same group unless waypoints is false. Elevations in the file are IGNORED — the line drapes on the loaded terrain exactly as viewer_draw_line does — but the range found in the file is reported so you can compare. A segment over 4096 points is thinned (Douglas-Peucker) to fit; pass simplify_m to choose the tolerance, or let it find the smallest that fits and say which it used. THEN CHECK IT: compare each returned flat length against the distance the source page states. Agreement to a few per cent is what turns "a line appeared" into "the right trail is drawn"; a mismatch over about 5% means the wrong track, a partial one, or a different variant of the route.

gpx_text.description: The raw GPX XML. Fetch it yourself; this tool does no network access

name.description: Base name; a file with several segments gets " #2", " #3" and so on. Default: the track own <name>

style.description: One of ghost | solid; default solid

group.description: A group name, for viewer_clear; default "tracks"

simplify_m.description: Douglas-Peucker tolerance in metres, 1-1000. Used only when a segment exceeds 4096 points

source.description: An attribution line — the site the track came from. Shown in the page sources panel for as long as the lines are drawn

waypoints.description: Turn <wpt> elements into markers; default true

tools.name: viewer_mark_buildings
tools.description: Colours every building footprint within radius_m of a point: a few metres (0.5-10) marks the one building under the coordinate, 500 m marks the whole neighbourhood. The test is exact (distance to the footprint ring, zero inside it). The mark is kept in a registry and applied to cells as they load, so it lights up when the camera gets there; hit counts footprints coloured now, pending counts cells not yet loaded. usage narrows to PLATEAU codes. PLATEAU usage codes: 401 offices, 402 retail, 411 detached housing, 412 apartments, 421 government, 422 education/culture/welfare (schools, universities, nurseries, hospitals, libraries — a class, not "schools"), 441 factories, 461 unknown. A usage filter matches nothing in version-1 tiles, which carry no usage. min_height_m/max_height_m narrow by height in metres. Filters by height are reliable in every tile version (unlike usage); a tower published as stacked slices counts by its whole structure height. min_ground_m/max_ground_m narrow by the footprint's ground above mean sea level: 'buildings under +10 m if the sea rose' is max_ground_m: 10 (and viewer_set_sea_rise 10 shows it). where is one filter over the format-3 building attributes: {attr: {min?, max?}} for numbers, {attr: [codes]} for code lists, {attr: true|false} for flags — attributes height, ground, storeys, year, flood, tide, tsunami (metres), usage, structure, fireproof (PLATEAU code strings), band, landslide, named. Examples: {"year": {"max": 1981}, "structure": ["601"]} (wooden, pre-1981 seismic code); {"flood": {"min": 3}} (river-flood depth 3 m or more). Coverage varies by city; a building whose record lacks the attribute never matches a bound on it (absent is null, never zero); format-1/2 sets answer null for all of these. The page validates where and refuses what it cannot read. label also places a marker at the point. Caps: 64 marks, 15 distinct colours per session. Colour with #rrggbb or a CSS name.

min_height_m.description: Only buildings at least this tall, metres 0-2000

max_height_m.description: Only buildings at most this tall, metres 0-2000

min_ground_m.description: Only buildings whose ground is at least this high above mean sea level, -50-3000

max_ground_m.description: Only buildings whose ground is at most this high above mean sea level, -50-3000

label.description: Also place a marker with this label at the point

tools.name: viewer_mark_polygon
tools.description: Colours every building whose centroid lies inside a ring of 3-256 lat/lon points, narrowed by usage codes and/or min_height_m/max_height_m and min_ground_m/max_ground_m if given. Applied to cells as they load, like viewer_mark_buildings. PLATEAU usage codes: 401 offices, 402 retail, 411 detached housing, 412 apartments, 421 government, 422 education/culture/welfare (schools, universities, nurseries, hospitals, libraries — a class, not "schools"), 441 factories, 461 unknown. A usage filter matches nothing in version-1 tiles, which carry no usage. Filters by height are reliable in every tile version (unlike usage); a tower published as stacked slices counts by its whole structure height. 'buildings under +10 m if the sea rose' is max_ground_m: 10 (and viewer_set_sea_rise 10 shows it). where is one filter over the format-3 building attributes: {attr: {min?, max?}} for numbers, {attr: [codes]} for code lists, {attr: true|false} for flags — attributes height, ground, storeys, year, flood, tide, tsunami (metres), usage, structure, fireproof (PLATEAU code strings), band, landslide, named. Examples: {"year": {"max": 1981}, "structure": ["601"]} (wooden, pre-1981 seismic code); {"flood": {"min": 3}} (river-flood depth 3 m or more). Coverage varies by city; a building whose record lacks the attribute never matches a bound on it (absent is null, never zero); format-1/2 sets answer null for all of these. The page validates where and refuses what it cannot read.

polygon.description: 3-256 points, a closed ring (do not repeat the first)

min_height_m.description: Only buildings at least this tall, metres 0-2000

max_height_m.description: Only buildings at most this tall, metres 0-2000

min_ground_m.description: Only buildings whose ground is at least this high above mean sea level, -50-3000

max_ground_m.description: Only buildings whose ground is at most this high above mean sea level, -50-3000

tools.name: viewer_query_buildings
tools.description: The buildings within radius_m of a point, from LOADED cells only: count, and the nearest ones with position, height, usage and distance (up to limit, default 50). pending says how many cells in the disc are not loaded yet — fly closer and ask again. This is how "which of these are schools" gets real footprints to reason about. PLATEAU usage codes: 401 offices, 402 retail, 411 detached housing, 412 apartments, 421 government, 422 education/culture/welfare (schools, universities, nurseries, hospitals, libraries — a class, not "schools"), 441 factories, 461 unknown. A usage filter matches nothing in version-1 tiles, which carry no usage. min_height_m/max_height_m narrow by height in metres; Filters by height are reliable in every tile version (unlike usage); a tower published as stacked slices counts by its whole structure height. min_ground_m/max_ground_m narrow by the footprint's ground above mean sea level (reported per building): 'buildings under +10 m if the sea rose' is max_ground_m: 10 (and viewer_set_sea_rise 10 shows it). where is one filter over the format-3 building attributes: {attr: {min?, max?}} for numbers, {attr: [codes]} for code lists, {attr: true|false} for flags — attributes height, ground, storeys, year, flood, tide, tsunami (metres), usage, structure, fireproof (PLATEAU code strings), band, landslide, named. Examples: {"year": {"max": 1981}, "structure": ["601"]} (wooden, pre-1981 seismic code); {"flood": {"min": 3}} (river-flood depth 3 m or more). Coverage varies by city; a building whose record lacks the attribute never matches a bound on it (absent is null, never zero); format-1/2 sets answer null for all of these. The page validates where and refuses what it cannot read. Records also carry the format-3 facts (storeys, year, structure, fireproof, flood/tide/tsunami depths, landslide, name) where the city delivered them. sort "height" lists the tallest first, so a capped list holds the tallest matches rather than the nearest.

min_height_m.description: Only buildings at least this tall, metres 0-2000

max_height_m.description: Only buildings at most this tall, metres 0-2000

min_ground_m.description: Only buildings whose ground is at least this high above mean sea level, -50-3000

max_ground_m.description: Only buildings whose ground is at most this high above mean sea level, -50-3000

sort.description: distance | height; default distance (nearest first); height = tallest first

tools.name: viewer_find_buildings
tools.description: Find buildings by name — PLATEAU names the landmarks (東京スカイツリー, 神田駅, 区立常盤小学校…), so this is how to mark or fly to a place without coordinates; then viewer_mark_buildings with a small radius, or viewer_go_to. The match is a case-insensitive substring over the loaded cells (one or two percent of buildings carry a name, and only in format-3 sets) AND, where the set publishes a name index, over every named building in the set: those come back with loaded: false and carry only name, position, structure height and usage until the camera loads their cell (viewer_go_to name flies there). lat, lon, radius_m together narrow to a disc and sort nearest first; without them the whole set is searched, by name. A where clause keeps the search to loaded cells — the index carries no attributes. where is one filter over the format-3 building attributes: {attr: {min?, max?}} for numbers, {attr: [codes]} for code lists, {attr: true|false} for flags — attributes height, ground, storeys, year, flood, tide, tsunami (metres), usage, structure, fireproof (PLATEAU code strings), band, landslide, named. Examples: {"year": {"max": 1981}, "structure": ["601"]} (wooden, pre-1981 seismic code); {"flood": {"min": 3}} (river-flood depth 3 m or more). Coverage varies by city; a building whose record lacks the attribute never matches a bound on it (absent is null, never zero); format-1/2 sets answer null for all of these. The page validates where and refuses what it cannot read.

name.description: 1-80 characters, matched case-insensitively as a substring

lat.description: With lon and radius_m: search only within this disc

tools.name: viewer_label_buildings
tools.description: Writes labels on the tallest buildings around a point — the picture that answers "which of these is which". The selection is the one viewer_query_buildings takes (radius_m 1-5000, usage, min_height_m/max_height_m, min_ground_m/max_ground_m, where), narrowed to the top tallest (1-32, default 8). named: true labels only buildings PLATEAU gave a name (one or two percent of them); text is "name", "height" or "both" (default: the name where there is one, else the height). A tower published as stacked slices is labelled ONCE, at its structure height, so Skytree reads 635 m rather than a stack of pieces. The labels are MARKERS in a group (default "labels"): viewer_clear kinds ["markers"] group labels takes them away, and they are painted into captures with the other overlays, so viewer_screenshot shows them. PLATEAU usage codes: 401 offices, 402 retail, 411 detached housing, 412 apartments, 421 government, 422 education/culture/welfare (schools, universities, nurseries, hospitals, libraries — a class, not "schools"), 441 factories, 461 unknown. A usage filter matches nothing in version-1 tiles, which carry no usage. Filters by height are reliable in every tile version (unlike usage); a tower published as stacked slices counts by its whole structure height. where is one filter over the format-3 building attributes: {attr: {min?, max?}} for numbers, {attr: [codes]} for code lists, {attr: true|false} for flags — attributes height, ground, storeys, year, flood, tide, tsunami (metres), usage, structure, fireproof (PLATEAU code strings), band, landslide, named. Examples: {"year": {"max": 1981}, "structure": ["601"]} (wooden, pre-1981 seismic code); {"flood": {"min": 3}} (river-flood depth 3 m or more). Coverage varies by city; a building whose record lacks the attribute never matches a bound on it (absent is null, never zero); format-1/2 sets answer null for all of these. The page validates where and refuses what it cannot read.

top.description: How many of the tallest to label, 1-32; default 8

named.description: Only buildings with a PLATEAU name; default false

text.description: name | height | both; default both (the name where there is one, else the height)

min_height_m.description: Only buildings at least this tall, metres 0-2000

max_height_m.description: Only buildings at most this tall, metres 0-2000

min_ground_m.description: Only buildings whose ground is at least this high above mean sea level, -50-3000

max_ground_m.description: Only buildings whose ground is at most this high above mean sea level, -50-3000

color.description: Label colour, #rrggbb or a CSS name

tools.name: viewer_area_stats
tools.description: The whole picture of an area in one call: a disc (lat, lon, radius_m) or a polygon (3-256 points). Buildings from loaded cells — count, by usage (decoded), height histogram, the tallest three with names, footprint area, storeys, years (quartiles, before/after the 1981 seismic code), structure and fireproofing, hazard shares and maxima, ground above sea; plus the land-cover mix (JAXA HRLULC) and the mean night radiance (VIIRS) over the same disc. PLATEAU usage codes: 401 offices, 402 retail, 411 detached housing, 412 apartments, 421 government, 422 education/culture/welfare (schools, universities, nurseries, hospitals, libraries — a class, not "schools"), 441 factories, 461 unknown. A usage filter matches nothing in version-1 tiles, which carry no usage. where is one filter over the format-3 building attributes: {attr: {min?, max?}} for numbers, {attr: [codes]} for code lists, {attr: true|false} for flags — attributes height, ground, storeys, year, flood, tide, tsunami (metres), usage, structure, fireproof (PLATEAU code strings), band, landslide, named. Examples: {"year": {"max": 1981}, "structure": ["601"]} (wooden, pre-1981 seismic code); {"flood": {"min": 3}} (river-flood depth 3 m or more). Coverage varies by city; a building whose record lacks the attribute never matches a bound on it (absent is null, never zero); format-1/2 sets answer null for all of these. The page validates where and refuses what it cannot read. Attributes a set does not carry are said plainly ("this set's tiles carry no year"). pending cells are not loaded yet — fly closer for the rest.

polygon.description: Instead of a disc: 3-256 points, a closed ring

usage.description: Only these PLATEAU usage codes, e.g. ["411", "412"]

tools.name: viewer_set_sea_rise
tools.description: Draws the sea rise_m metres above the local mean sea level, so low ground floods and buildings stand in water: a bathtub picture, not a hazard model; buildings and heights still report against the real sea. 0 restores the real sea. Pair it with max_ground_m on viewer_mark_buildings / viewer_query_buildings, or a ground theme from viewer_theme_buildings, to show what stands below the line. A set without a geoid grid draws no sea at all.

rise_m.description: Metres above mean sea level, -50-100; 0 = the real sea

tools.name: viewer_set_field
tools.description: Colours buildings by a national raster on the ground instead of by a per-building pass. viewer_theme_buildings walks the loaded cells and writes a colour into every vertex, so it reaches as far as the geometry does and pays that walk again on each cell that loads. A field is a texture lookup in the shader: nothing per building, nothing per cell, nothing to re-upload when the bins change, and a cell that loads later is already the right colour. Use it for anything that is a grid rather than a property of a building - measured light, and population when it is published. It cannot colour a building that is not drawn: the geometry budget still decides what exists, and at altitude that is the large buildings. bins are in the source's own units, ascending, and colors needs bins + 1 entries. source "off" clears it. A theme, being about buildings someone asked for, still wins where both apply.

source.description: One of nightlights | off; default nightlights

bins.description: Required unless source is "off": ascending upper bounds in the source's units, at most 8

mix.description: How far the field colours a building, 0-1; default 1

tools.name: viewer_theme_buildings
tools.description: A theme: every loaded building (or those within a disc when lat, lon, radius_m are given) coloured by an attribute through a ramp, with a legend painted on the page. Numeric attributes bin by ascending `bins` upper bounds (value < bins[0] takes colour 0, ... >= the last takes the last colour), so colors has bins.length + 1 entries; usage themes bin by `classes` (a list of code lists) with one colour each. Default colours: a blue-to-red ramp. Examples: colour buildings graded by height: by height, bins [10, 20, 40, 60, 100]; by ground elevation for a sea-rise picture: by ground, bins [0, 2, 5, 10]; by class: by usage, classes [["411","412"],["401","402"],["422"]]; by year, bins [1981, 2000, 2011]; by flood, bins [0.5, 3, 5]; by structure, classes [["601"],["603","602"],["604","605"]]. Numeric attributes (height, structure_height, ground, band, storeys, year, flood, tide, tsunami) take bins; usage, structure and fireproof take classes of PLATEAU code strings. Legend units come from the page. Themes clear with the marks. TWO ATTRIBUTES AT ONCE: secondary_by (usage, structure or fireproof) with secondary_classes adds a second channel — the first attribute picks how deep the colour is, the second picks the hue, which is the standard bivariate map and the way to read exposure against consequence in one picture. The case this is for: by flood, bins [0.5, 1.5, 3], secondary_by usage, secondary_classes [["411","412"],["422"]] — flood depth against housing versus hospitals and schools. It needs bins x classes colours (at most 31), and the default palette generates them. A building the second channel does not classify is left uncoloured rather than folded into a class it is not in. PLATEAU usage codes: 401 offices, 402 retail, 411 detached housing, 412 apartments, 421 government, 422 education/culture/welfare (schools, universities, nurseries, hospitals, libraries — a class, not "schools"), 441 factories, 461 unknown. A usage filter matches nothing in version-1 tiles, which carry no usage. where is one filter over the format-3 building attributes: {attr: {min?, max?}} for numbers, {attr: [codes]} for code lists, {attr: true|false} for flags — attributes height, ground, storeys, year, flood, tide, tsunami (metres), usage, structure, fireproof (PLATEAU code strings), band, landslide, named. Examples: {"year": {"max": 1981}, "structure": ["601"]} (wooden, pre-1981 seismic code); {"flood": {"min": 3}} (river-flood depth 3 m or more). Coverage varies by city; a building whose record lacks the attribute never matches a bound on it (absent is null, never zero); format-1/2 sets answer null for all of these. The page validates where and refuses what it cannot read.

by.description: One of height | structure_height | ground | band | usage | storeys | year | flood | tide | tsunami | structure | fireproof

bins.description: Ascending upper bounds for a numeric attribute, at most 11

colors.description: #rrggbb or CSS names; bins.length + 1 for numeric, classes.length for usage; at most 31

classes.description: For by usage / structure / fireproof: one list of PLATEAU codes per bin

secondary_by.description: A second channel read as hue: one of usage | structure | fireproof. Must differ from by

secondary_classes.description: For secondary_by: 1-6 lists of PLATEAU codes, one hue each

where.description: Attribute filter applied before binning, e.g. {"named": true}

lat.description: With lon and radius_m: theme only within this disc

tools.name: viewer_terrain_profile
tools.description: The ground's height along a path of 2-512 lat/lon points, sampled every step_m (default about 20 m): length, climb and descent, lowest and highest ground, and a compact list of samples. Heights are above mean sea level where the geoid is published, else ellipsoidal. Answers from the tiles in memory: fly there first, then ask.

tools.name: viewer_measure
tools.description: Distances along 2-512 lat/lon points: each leg, the total flat, and the total along the draped ground; closed: true (or area: true with 3+ points) also gives the enclosed area, planar in a local frame. Answers from the tiles in memory: fly there first, then ask.

closed.description: Close the ring back to the first point; default false

area.description: Also report the enclosed area (3+ points); default false

tools.name: viewer_viewshed
tools.description: The ground visible from a viewpoint (eye_height_m above the ground there) within radius_m, with earth curvature and standard refraction: the visible fraction, how far the visible horizon reaches, and — with draw (default true) — the horizon drawn on the ground as a line named "viewshed N m" in group "viewshed", cleared with viewer_clear. Answers from the tiles in memory: fly there first, then ask. The viewpoint's own ground must be loaded.

eye_height_m.description: Eye above the ground, 0-500 m; default 1.7

draw.description: Draw the visible horizon as a line; default true

color.description: Line colour, #rrggbb or a CSS name; default yellow

tools.name: viewer_terrain_overlays
tools.description: Contour lines every contours_m metres (0-1000; 0 switches them off) and a red tint on steep ground (slope: true/false), drawn by the terrain shader on whatever tiles are loaded. Give one or both.

tools.name: viewer_landcover
tools.description: The land-cover classes within radius_m of a point (default 1000 m), largest first, with their share and area: water, built-up, paddy, cropland, grassland, four forest classes, bare, bamboo, solar panel, wetland, greenhouse (JAXA HRLULC, 10 m at the finest level, coarser far from the camera). Answers from the tiles in memory: fly there first, then ask.

tools.name: viewer_nightlights
tools.description: Night-time radiance within radius_m of a point (default 5000 m): mean and maximum in nW/cm²/sr and the lit fraction (texels at 1 nW/cm²/sr or more). VIIRS annual night-time radiance, ≈1.3 km texels — a measurement of light at night, not of population. Refused when the set carries no night lights.

tools.name: viewer_nightlights_at
tools.description: Night-time radiance under up to 256 points, in nW/cm²/sr; null outside the published grid. VIIRS annual night-time radiance, ≈1.3 km texels — a measurement of light at night, not of population. Refused when the set carries no night lights.

tools.name: viewer_query_paths
tools.description: The footpaths and stone steps near a point, with elevations. There is no separate trail layer: the road set is MLIT N13 centrelines, and its band 3 is 徒歩道 (footpaths) and 石段 (stone steps). N13 carries no names or refs (a "Trail 6" must be matched by where it runs) and its horizontal accuracy is about 25 m. Band 3 only loads within about 6 km of the camera: fly there first, then ask. A NAMED trail (Trail 6, 稲荷山コース, a route out of a guidebook) is not something this layer can give you: N13 has the geometry but no names, so the best it can do is a shape that resembles the route. Get the real one from the web instead — route-wiki sites such as Yamareco publish a GPX download per named route — and draw its coordinates with viewer_draw_line. Then check it: compare the returned length2d against the distance the source states, and treat a mismatch over about 5% as the wrong or a partial track. For an unnamed, exploratory ask ("show the hiking paths around this valley") N13 is the right answer and wants no web. Returns the nearest paths (up to limit, default 20) until max_points vertices are spent; each has id, kind, flags, distance, 2D length and elevations. To draw one, call viewer_draw_paths with its id — no coordinates needed. include_points: true prints each path's [lat, lon, h] points in the text (they are always in the structured result, which hosts may not show). pending counts meshes in range whose band 3 is not loaded yet — fly closer and ask again.

include_points.description: Print each path's [lat, lon, h] points in the text; default false

tools.name: viewer_draw_paths
tools.description: Draws footpaths or steps from viewer_query_paths by their ids: the page draws each from its own resident geometry, draped on the terrain like viewer_draw_line and re-draped as tiles land, so no coordinates cross the companion or the model. 1-64 ids per call; color as #rrggbb or a CSS name, width_px 1-12, style ghost | solid, group (default "paths") for viewer_clear. An id whose cell has been evicted since the query comes back as missing — query again near it.

group.description: A group name, for viewer_clear; default "paths"

tools.name: viewer_route_path
tools.description: "Walk from A to B", "the trail from the station to the summit": a route between two points along the loaded footpaths, with its length, climb and descent, drawn on the ground and charted. The route runs ONLY along footpaths and steps (N13 band 3: 徒歩道 and 石段), never along roads, and only where those cells are loaded — band 3 is resident within about 6 km of the camera, so fly there first. Two trails with a road between them are not joined: the route refuses and says so. A NAMED trail (Trail 6, 稲荷山コース, a route out of a guidebook) is not something this layer can give you: N13 has the geometry but no names, so the best it can do is a shape that resembles the route. Get the real one from the web instead — route-wiki sites such as Yamareco publish a GPX download per named route — and draw its coordinates with viewer_draw_line. Then check it: compare the returned length2d against the distance the source states, and treat a mismatch over about 5% as the wrong or a partial track. For an unnamed, exploratory ask ("show the hiking paths around this valley") N13 is the right answer and wants no web. Each end snaps to the nearest footpath node within snap_m (5-2000, default 100); a snap over 30 m means the point was not on a path. draw (default true) draws the route as a solid line in group "routes"; bands defaults to [3] — footpaths and steps only. Add the driven bands ([0,1,2,3]) when a walk refuses in a city: pavements there are published as part of the road, not as footpaths, so band 3 alone can find nothing between two points a few metres apart. The result then says it is road-network routing, and it means it — a carriageway centreline carries no pavement, no crossing and no direction of travel, so report it as a road distance rather than as a walking route. profile (default true) puts its elevation chart on the page (bottom right, and in screenshots) until viewer_clear kinds ["profile"]. The route id (route:n) can be flown with viewer_follow_path trace_id and is dropped by viewer_clear kinds ["traces"].

snap_m.description: How far an end may be from a footpath node, 5-2000 m; default 100

bands.description: Which road bands to route along: [3] (default) is footpaths and steps only; [0,1,2,3] adds the driven network, which is ROAD-NETWORK routing and not a walkable path

draw.description: Draw the route as a solid line in group "routes"; default true

color.description: Line colour, #rrggbb or a CSS name

profile.description: Show the elevation chart; default true

title.description: The chart's title, at most 60 characters; default the route id

tools.name: viewer_show_profile
tools.description: "Show the profile", "how much climb is that": an elevation chart (distance against height) drawn bottom right of the page and into every screenshot with overlays, for a footpath (path_id from viewer_query_paths), a drawn line (line_id), a road trace or a footpath route (trace_id from viewer_follow_road / viewer_route_path), or 2-4096 points sampled on the loaded ground. Exactly one source. Returns length, climb, descent, the lowest and highest height and the sample count. One chart at a time — a new one replaces it; viewer_clear kinds ["profile"] removes it. Points need loaded ground under at least two of them: fly there first.

trace_id.description: A trace id from viewer_follow_road or a route id from viewer_route_path

line_id.description: A line id from viewer_draw_line / viewer_draw_paths

points.description: 2-4096 [lat, lon] points instead of an id

title.description: At most 60 characters; default the source's id

tools.name: viewer_follow_road
tools.description: "Follow the E20 from Tokyo", "fly along the expressway to Kōfu": traces a trunk road through ordered waypoints and flies along it agl_m (default 300, 50-5000) above the ground, looking ahead down the road. The road is found from your waypoints: N13 carries no route names or numbers (no "E20", no "国道20号"), so the page traces the trunk network (expressways and 国道) through the waypoints you give, in order. Two rules, and the second is the one that bites. (1) EVERY WAYPOINT MUST SIT ON THE CARRIAGEWAY — an interchange, not the town beside it. One that is off the road drags the trace onto a 国道 to reach it: measured Tokyo-Kōfu, the two ends alone give 113 km all on toll road (the real Chūō Expressway), while eight approximate interchanges give 152 km with a fifth on national roads. (2) HOW MANY depends on how straight the road runs. Only a corridor three meshes wide — roughly 11-22 km — around the straight line between CONSECUTIVE waypoints is fetched, so a road that bends further out than that is not in the graph at all. Two ends are enough when the road runs roughly straight between them; otherwise give one on the carriageway every 50-100 km to steer the corridor along the road. Measured: Tokyo-Osaka on its two ends REFUSES — the straight line crosses the mountains while the Tōmei follows the coast — and on seven real interchanges traces 559.7 km at 0.87 toll over 146 meshes in about a second. prefer "expressway" (default) prices non-toll road at four times, so the router finds the toll road on its own; "any" takes the shortest trunk route. A leg whose ends do not connect within that corridor is refused with its leg number, and the fix is a waypoint on the carriageway between those two. Pace: speed_mps (default 120 m/s — a 120 km leg takes about 17 min) or fly_s (1-3600) for the whole flight; the result says how long it took. draw (default true) draws the trace as a ghost ribbon in group "follow" first. clock/season may scrub across the flight; caption rides on it. This call returns when the flight ends, so it can run for many minutes; interrupted means the person took the camera — do not fly again without asking. The result lists the length, each leg's snap distances (a snap over 500 m means the waypoint was off the road), and how the flight ended.

waypoints.description: 2-32 [lat, lon] points, in order, EACH ON THE CARRIAGEWAY (an interchange, not the town beside it): the two ends when the road runs roughly straight between them, else one every 50-100 km to steer the corridor along the road

agl_m.description: Height above the ground, 50-5000 m; default 300

fly_s.description: Whole flight in seconds, 1-3600, instead of a speed

prefer.description: expressway | any; default expressway (keeps to toll roads)

snap_m.description: How far a waypoint may be from the trunk network, 100-10000 m; default 3000

look_ahead_m.description: Aim this far ahead on the road, 0-5000 m; default 800

draw.description: Draw the trace as a ghost ribbon first; default true

color.description: Ribbon colour, #rrggbb or a CSS name

caption.description: A caption shown during the flight and cleared after, at most 240 characters

clock.description: JST hours, "HH:MM", or a solar token (sunrise, golden_hour_pm, sunset-0:20 ...) resolved where this call is aimed; or [from, to] scrubbed across the flight

season.description: Day of year or "MM-DD"; or [from, to]

clouds.description: One of clear | scattered | fair | overcast

tools.name: viewer_follow_path
tools.description: Flies along something already on the page — a footpath by path_id (from viewer_query_paths), a drawn line by line_id, a road trace or a footpath route by trace_id (a trace id from viewer_follow_road or a route id from viewer_route_path), or a list of points — agl_m above the ground (default 300), looking ahead along it. Exactly one source. Pace: speed_mps (default 120) or fly_s (1-3600); a trail at 120 m/s is too fast — 20-40 m/s reads. The page resolves the geometry itself, so no coordinates need to cross for an id. Returns when the flight ends (the wait is capped at one hour; give seconds for a path of unknown length); interrupted means the person took the camera — do not fly again without asking.

path_id.description: A footpath id from viewer_query_paths, e.g. "533945:3:12"

line_id.description: A line id from viewer_draw_line / viewer_draw_paths

trace_id.description: A trace id from viewer_follow_road, e.g. "trace:1"

points.description: 2-4096 [lat, lon] points instead of an id

agl_m.description: Height above the ground, 50-5000 m; default 300

fly_s.description: Whole flight in seconds, 1-3600, instead of a speed

look_ahead_m.description: Aim this far ahead, 0-5000 m; default 800

caption.description: A caption shown during the flight and cleared after, at most 240 characters

clock.description: JST hours, "HH:MM", or a solar token (sunrise, golden_hour_pm, sunset-0:20 ...) resolved where this call is aimed; or [from, to] scrubbed across the flight

season.description: Day of year or "MM-DD"; or [from, to]

clouds.description: One of clear | scattered | fair | overcast

tools.name: viewer_export_scene
tools.description: Everything the tools have put on the viewer — camera, clock, season, clouds, marks, lines, markers and caption — as one JSON document. Save it as a .json file and drop it onto the viewer later to restore it with no assistant in the room, or pass it back to viewer_load_scene.

tools.name: viewer_load_scene
tools.description: A document from viewer_export_scene (kind "ss-geodata-scene"), or the name of a scene saved with viewer_save_scene, applied whole: everything drawn is cleared first, then the camera, time, sky and every annotation are restored. Give scene or name, not both. Returns the counts restored.

name.description: The name of a saved scene (viewer_list_scenes)

tools.name: viewer_save_scene
tools.description: Saves everything on the viewer (camera, clock, season, clouds, marks, lines, markers, caption) as a named scene on disk — the safety net before a demo, the way back after an experiment. name is letters, digits, _ and - (at most 60), never a path; a name already saved is replaced. viewer_list_scenes lists them, viewer_load_scene name restores one.

tools.name: viewer_list_scenes
tools.description: The scenes saved by viewer_save_scene: name, when it was saved, and how many marks, lines and markers it holds. Needs no page.

tools.name: viewer_set_time
tools.description: Sets the time of day and/or the day of year, which drive the sun, the moon, the sky and the shadows. clock is JST hours 0-24, "HH:MM", or a solar token; season is a day of year 0-364 or "MM-DD" (a year prefix is ignored). At least one is required. Either may be [from, to]: with over_s the camera holds still and the day (or the year) runs past it over that many seconds — a time-lapse from where you are.

clock.description: JST hours 0-24, "HH:MM", a solar token, or [from, to] with over_s

season.description: Day of year 0-364, "MM-DD" / "YYYY-MM-DD", or [from, to] with over_s

over_s.description: Run a [from, to] scrub past the held camera over this many seconds, 0.2-120

tools.name: viewer_sun_events
tools.description: When the sun rises and sets at a place on a day, JST — from the same arithmetic the viewer lights the scene with, so the clock values drop straight into viewer_set_time or a clock scrub: civil dawn and dusk (sun 6° below the horizon: the blue hour), sunrise and sunset (−0.833°, the upper limb on the horizon), the end of the morning golden hour and the start of the evening one (sun 6° up), solar noon and its elevation. Needs no page. "Show me X at sunset" = viewer_sun_events, then viewer_set_time with the suggested clock (or the scrub on a flight). Japan only (lat 20-46); the longitude matters — Sendai's sun runs 23 minutes ahead of Akashi's.

tools.name: viewer_set_sky
tools.description: Cloud cover by name (clear, scattered, fair, overcast) and/or render quality (balanced, high, ultra). The page owns the names and refuses one it does not know. At least one is required.

clouds.description: One of clear | scattered | fair | overcast

tools.name: viewer_set_layers
tools.description: Switches any of the layers on or off: roads, buildings, landcover, vegetation, sea, shadows, nightlights, hud, footpaths. Only the keys given change. roads is the whole N13 road network; footpaths is its band 3 alone (徒歩道 footpaths and 石段 steps — there is no separate trail layer). Returns the full layers block afterwards.

tools.name: viewer_wait_settled
tools.description: Waits until tiles have stopped arriving and the frame is steady (the film kit's quiet condition), or until timeout_s (default 20, at most 120). Returns how long it took and whether it timed out.

tools.name: viewer_screenshot
tools.description: A JPEG of the current frame with the required credits composited in, as an image. width 320-3840 (default 1280); settle (default true) waits for the scene to be steady first, bounded by timeout_s (default 30). The capture includes the caption, markers with labels, and the current theme's legend, so you see your own annotations; overlays: false gives the bare frame (credits stay). Use it to verify what a camera, time or layer change produced. keep: "name" also keeps the frame on the page under that name (at most 4; a repeated name replaces) for viewer_compose_screenshots; viewer_clear kinds ["shots"] drops them.

settle.description: Wait for the scene to settle first; default true

overlays.description: Paint the caption, markers and legend into the capture; default true

keep.description: Also keep the frame on the page under this name (^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,40}$) for viewer_compose_screenshots

tools.name: viewer_compose_screenshots
tools.description: Draws 2-4 screenshots kept on the page (viewer_screenshot with keep: "name") into one JPEG, side by side (layout "side", default) or stacked ("stack"), with a label strip over each — theme A vs theme B, marks vs none, any before/after that viewer_compare does not cover. labels default to the names. A name not kept is refused. width 320-3840 (default 1280). Kept shots go with viewer_clear kinds ["shots"].

labels.description: One per name, at most 40 characters each; default the names

tools.name: viewer_compare
tools.description: Before/after from the same camera: two state patches a and b, each any of clock, season, clouds, sea_rise_m, layers ({roads, buildings, ...}); an empty patch is the viewer as it is now. Each is applied, the scene settled and captured, the two frames composed into one image (layout side | stack) with labels (default derived: "06:00" / "19:00", "sea +5 m", "buildings off"), and then everything the patches changed is put back as it was. Examples: dawn vs dusk {a: {clock: "06:00"}, b: {clock: "19:00"}}; sea rise {a: {}, b: {sea_rise_m: 5}}; summer vs winter {a: {season: "07-01"}, b: {season: "01-15"}}. Takes two settles, so allow a minute.

a.description: Left/top state: any of clock, season, clouds, sea_rise_m, layers

b.description: Right/bottom state: any of clock, season, clouds, sea_rise_m, layers

labels.description: Two labels, at most 40 characters each; default derived from the patches

tools.name: viewer_places
tools.description: Looks a name up in everything this set can resolve: the viewer's own short list of landmarks, and the national index of buildings PLATEAU names — stations, towers, halls, schools. With no query it lists the short list and the published extent. This is the whole gazetteer: there is no index of summits, districts, wards or bays, so those still need coordinates, and this says so rather than guessing at one. A building answer carries loaded: false when it is in the index but not in memory — flying there loads it.

query.description: Part of a name, matched case-insensitively; omitted lists the short list

tools.name: viewer_clear
tools.description: Removes annotations, by id, by group, or by kind — the three ways of naming the same things. ids takes exactly those (any id from viewer_list_annotations: a mark, a theme, a line, a marker, a trace, a kept frame, "profile", "caption") and nothing else. group takes everything in a group. kinds (marks, lines, markers, caption, traces, shots, profile) takes whole registries, and with no arguments at all it clears everything drawn by tools. Clearing marks removes the colour from every loaded cell, and clearing all of them frees the mark palette. Returns what was removed, and which ids were not found.

ids.description: Clear exactly these annotation ids, from viewer_list_annotations. Not with group or kinds

kinds.description: Any of marks, lines, markers, caption, traces, shots, profile

tools.name: viewer_batch
tools.description: Runs up to 16 viewer calls in order, in one round trip: [{tool, args}, ...]. Made for choreography — set the time, theme the buildings, put a caption up, take the screenshot — where each step is cheap and the round trips are most of the cost. Fail-fast: the first refusal stops the run, and the answer says which step failed, what it said, and how many were not attempted. Each step's own text and images come back under its number; the scene is reported once at the end, for the state the run finished in. Read-only calls are fine in a batch, but a batch is not a transaction — steps that already ran are not undone. viewer_batch cannot call itself.

args.description: That tool's arguments; omitted means none

tools.name: viewer_list_annotations
tools.description: One list of everything on the page that a tool put there — marks, themes, lines, markers, road traces and routes, kept frames, the profile chart, the caption — each with the id and group viewer_clear takes. Use it before clearing selectively, or to see what a long sequence has accumulated. Also reports what is used of each session cap.

instructions:
You are driving a 3D viewer of Japan (terrain, buildings, roads, land cover, sky) over a local bridge the person enabled by hand. Conventions, which every tool and shot file share:
- lat/lon are WGS84 degrees. The published set covers Japan only: lat 20-46, lon 122-154.
- alt is metres above the ellipsoid, clamped 120 m - 900 km.
- Every argument says its unit in its name: _deg for angles, _s for seconds, _m for metres, _mps for speed, _px for pixels. So yaw_deg, pitch_deg, fly_s, hold_s, radius_m, width_px — never a bare yaw, pitch or seconds. The exception is a shot file, whose fields are the page's own (seconds, yaw, pitch).
- yaw_deg is compass degrees: 0 north, 90 east.
- pitch_deg is degrees below the horizon; negative looks up; clamped to +/-86. A solved viewpoint looks down 25 degrees by default, a travelling camera 22.
- clock is JST hours 0-24 (or "HH:MM"); season is a day of year 0-364 (or "MM-DD").
- Cloud names: clear, scattered, fair, overcast. Quality: balanced, high, ultra.
- 'Go to X' / 'show me X' -> viewer_go_to (flies to a viewpoint and looks at X). viewer_fly_to and viewer_set_camera place the camera itself and keep its aim unless look_at is given. viewer_orbit circles a place.
- A narrated tour of several places is ONE viewer_tour call, not a series of flights and captions; a caption on a single flight rides on the flight itself.
- A scrub such as clock: ["06:00", "19:00"] runs the day across one flight; season scrubs the same way.
- Ask for the light by name, not by guessing a time: clock accepts sunrise, golden_hour_am, noon, golden_hour_pm, sunset, blue_hour, civil_dawn, civil_dusk and night, with an offset (sunset-0:20, sunrise+45m, noon+2h). Each is resolved at the place the call is aimed at and on the day it will be seen, so "golden hour" is a different clock in Sapporo than in Naha and a different one again in January. Prefer these to a wall-clock time whenever the light is what matters.
- Every call that changes the scene answers with a `scene:` line — clock, sun elevation, season, sky, camera, layers, what is drawn, tiles still arriving. Read it instead of remembering what you set: the clock and the season persist between calls, and a season set once is inherited by everything after it. A `warning:` line is a cross-check that failed (a stop clocked after dusk, a frame solved on unloaded ground); the structured answer carries the same as `scene`, `warnings` and `notes`.
- Heights come from loaded tiles: fly first, then ask. viewer_ground_height answers null, and a line or marker sits on the ellipsoid, where the camera has not been; viewer_frame and viewer_orbit sample the ground under their target for you and re-frame once it loads.
- Terrain questions - how high, how steep, what can be seen, how far - are viewer_terrain_profile / viewer_measure / viewer_viewshed / viewer_terrain_overlays; all answer from loaded tiles, so fly there first.
- What covers the ground / how bright it is at night -> viewer_landcover / viewer_nightlights (JAXA land cover, VIIRS radiance: a measurement of light, not of population).
- Building usage (PLATEAU codes, version-2 tiles): 401 office, 402 retail, 411 detached housing, 412 apartments, 421 government, 422 education/culture/welfare (schools, universities, nurseries, hospitals, libraries — a class, not "schools"), 441 factory, 461 unknown. Usage filters match nothing in version-1 tiles. viewer_mark_buildings colours footprints around a point; viewer_query_buildings lists them with heights and usage from loaded cells; viewer_export_scene keeps everything drawn.
- 'Mark buildings taller than X near Y' -> viewer_mark_buildings with min_height_m; 'the N tallest near Y' -> viewer_query_buildings with sort height; 'label them' / 'which one is which' -> viewer_label_buildings (markers in a group, painted into screenshots).
- where filters on the format-3 attributes (storeys, year, flood/tide/tsunami depths, structure, fireproof, landslide, named) on every building tool: {"year": {"max": 1981}, "structure": ["601"]}; absent is null and never matches a bound, and coverage varies by city.
- Know the name, not the coordinates -> viewer_find_buildings, then viewer_go_to or viewer_mark_buildings (PLATEAU names landmarks, stations, schools: one or two percent of buildings).
- 'Go to <landmark name>' -> viewer_go_to with name when the place is a building (a station, a tower, a hall, a school): the name is resolved through the loaded cells and the set's national name index, an exact match preferred; coordinates still for anything else (a summit, a bay, a district). A found building with loaded: false is in the index but not loaded yet — flying there loads it.
- Sea rise / flooding pictures: viewer_set_sea_rise plus max_ground_m filters or a ground theme. Graded colouring: viewer_theme_buildings. The raised sea is a bathtub picture, not a hazard model.
- Trails: viewer_query_paths lists the N13 footpaths/steps near a point; viewer_draw_paths draws them by id (no coordinates need to cross). N13 has no names (~25 m accuracy); there is no separate trail layer, and footpaths only load within about 6 km of the camera: fly there first, then ask.
- A trail asked for BY NAME ('draw Trail 6', 'the trails of Mt. Takao') is the one case where the built-in layer is the wrong tool, because N13 carries no names and cannot be checked against one. Instead: find a GPX track on the web (route-wiki sites such as Yamareco publish one per named route), hand the XML to viewer_import_track, and verify — the drawn flat length against the distance the source states, with a mismatch over about 5% meaning the wrong or a partial track. Then mark the summit with viewer_places or viewer_find_buildings. Unnamed paths ("what hiking paths are around here") stay with viewer_query_paths.
- 'What is that building?' -> viewer_identify (the building under a screen point, default the centre, or at a coordinate); 'what am I looking at?' -> viewer_describe (the whole frame in words and numbers). Both answer from loaded cells: null with a reason means fly closer.
- Relative moves - 'a bit more to the left', 'zoom in', 'higher', 'look down' -> viewer_nudge, deltas from the camera as it is now.
- Before/after - dawn vs dusk, the sea +5 m vs now, a layer on vs off -> ONE viewer_compare call with two state patches (it captures both from the same camera, composes them, and restores the state). Anything else side by side: viewer_screenshot with keep, then viewer_compose_screenshots.
- Sunset / sunrise / golden hour / blue hour -> viewer_sun_events for the place and date (needs no page), then viewer_set_time with the clock it suggests, or its scrub on a flight.
- 'Follow the E20' / 'fly along the expressway to Kofu' -> viewer_follow_road. The data carries no route names or numbers, so the waypoints ARE the route, and every one must sit ON THE CARRIAGEWAY (an interchange, not the town beside it) or it drags the trace onto a national road to reach it. How many depends on how straight the road runs: only a corridor about 11-22 km wide around the straight line between consecutive waypoints is fetched, so two ends do for Tokyo-Kofu, but Tokyo-Osaka refuses on two and needs about seven, one every 50-100 km. prefer expressway finds the toll road on its own. A trail or a drawn line: viewer_follow_path by id. Both return when the flight ends, so say how long it will take or give fly_s.
- Counts, heights, ages, hazard, land cover and light for an area -> viewer_area_stats (a disc or a polygon).
- Scenes by name: viewer_save_scene before an experiment or a demo, viewer_list_scenes, viewer_load_scene name to go back.
- 'Render a video / make an MP4 of this flight' -> viewer_render_film (writes the shot list and spawns the offline renderer detached; it needs no page connection, but a serve must be up for the Chrome it opens), then viewer_film_jobs for progress and the encode. A 4K render is an overnight job; width 960 at 10 fps is the draft.
- 'Walk / hike from A to B', 'the trail from the station to the summit' -> viewer_route_path: along footpaths and steps only (never roads), through loaded cells only (fly there first); it draws the route and its elevation chart, and viewer_follow_path trace_id flies it. 'Show the profile' / 'how much climb' -> viewer_show_profile on a trail, line, route or points, or viewer_route_path's own chart; viewer_clear kinds ["profile"] removes it.
- Before planning work that needs a building attribute (year, structure, usage, a hazard depth) -> viewer_coverage: which of them this city actually fills in is a property of its PLATEAU delivery, not of the format, and absent is null, which no filter matches. Two attributes in one picture -> viewer_theme_buildings with secondary_by / secondary_classes (depth of colour says one, hue says the other).
- Ground the camera has never been near is not loaded -> viewer_preload fetches it without flying; a frame solved without it sits at 0 m, inside any hill. viewer_tour preloads its own stops.
- The matching buildings themselves, not a count of them -> viewer_export_buildings writes GeoJSON to a file.
- A choreographed sequence (set time, theme, caption, screenshot) -> ONE viewer_batch call, fail-fast, one scene reported at the end. What is drawn -> viewer_list_annotations; viewer_clear takes ids, a group or kinds.
Start with viewer_capabilities in a fresh session: it states the conventions, the tokens, the refusal codes and the caps in one call, and answers with no page attached. Then viewer_status: every other tool needs an attached page, and a "not-connected" refusal means the person has to press the LLM chip (or M) in the viewer. After changing the camera, time or layers, call viewer_screenshot to verify what it produced rather than assuming. Quote the attribution strings from viewer_state when describing sources. The shot files under ss-geodata://shots/ are worked examples of framing that has been scouted; ss-geodata://readme explains their fields.
